subject: creative-arts-sp
description: Creative Arts Senior Phase (Grades 7–9) question bank. One 20-item pool per atomic skill (the topic key IS the skill id). Content subject: 0.6 pass mark, mastery via lib/content-mastery.ts. Tap-only; no free text. Music + Visual Arts only.

CA.G7.MUL.A1.title: Note values and rests
CA.G7.MUL.A1.description: Music (CAPS G7) — Music literacy: Note values and rests.
CA.G7.MUL.A1.recovery_strategy: A note's value tells you how many beats it lasts; a semibreve is longest, a quaver short.

questions.question: Which note lasts the LONGEST?
questions.memo: A semibreve is worth four beats — the longest of the common note values.

questions.question: How many beats is a crotchet worth (in 4/4 time)?
questions.memo: A crotchet is one beat — the steady 'walking' beat of most music.

questions.question: How many beats is a minim worth?
questions.memo: A minim lasts two beats — twice as long as a crotchet.

questions.question: How many quavers fit into one crotchet beat?
questions.memo: A quaver is half a beat, so two quavers fill one crotchet beat.

questions.question: A rest is a symbol that tells you to be silent for a certain number of beats.
questions.memo: Rests are silences — each note value has a matching rest of the same length.

questions.question: A dot written after a note does what to its length?
options: Adds half of the note's value again
questions.expected: Adds half of the note's value again
questions.memo: A dot adds half the note's value: a dotted minim (2+1) lasts three beats.

questions.question: How many beats is a dotted minim worth?
questions.memo: A minim (2) plus its dot (half of 2 = 1) makes three beats.

questions.question: A note worth four beats is called a ____.
questions.memo: The semibreve is the four-beat note.

questions.question: A silence that lasts as long as a note is called a ____.
questions.memo: A rest is the silence; every note value has a matching rest.

questions.question: Which is the correct order from LONGEST to SHORTEST?
questions.memo: Each value is half the one before: semibreve (4), minim (2), crotchet (1), quaver (½).

questions.question: Two minims last the same total time as one semibreve.
questions.memo: Two minims (2+2) equal four beats, the same as a semibreve.

questions.question: How many crotchets equal one semibreve?
questions.memo: A semibreve is four beats, so four one-beat crotchets fill it.

questions.question: A quaver lasts longer than a crotchet.
questions.memo: A quaver is HALF a beat — shorter than a one-beat crotchet.

questions.question: A crotchet rest means you should…
questions.memo: A crotchet rest is one beat of silence.

questions.question: A note worth half a beat is a ____.
questions.memo: The quaver is the half-beat note.

questions.question: How many quavers are there in one semibreve?
questions.memo: A semibreve is four beats and each beat holds two quavers, so 4 × 2 = 8.

questions.question: A minim and a crotchet together last three beats.
questions.memo: Minim (2) plus crotchet (1) makes three beats.

questions.question: Which note value is shown with a hollow (open) note-head and a stem?
questions.memo: A minim has an open note-head with a stem; a semibreve has an open head with NO stem.

questions.question: Sort each symbol into a NOTE (sound) or a REST (silence).
questions.expected: Crotchets and minims are notes (sound); the 'rest' symbols are silences.
questions.memo: If the word 'rest' is in the name, it is a silence; otherwise it is a sounding note.

questions.question: Put these note values in order from LONGEST to SHORTEST.
questions.expected: Semibreve, minim, crotchet, quaver — each is half the length of the one before.
questions.memo: The values halve each time: 4, 2, 1, ½ beats.

CA.G7.MUL.A2.title: Treble and bass clef
CA.G7.MUL.A2.description: Music (CAPS G7) — Music literacy: Treble and bass clef.
CA.G7.MUL.A2.recovery_strategy: The clef at the start of a staff tells you which note each line and space stands for.

questions.question: What does a clef at the start of a staff tell you?
options: Which pitch each line and space stands for
questions.expected: Which pitch each line and space stands for
questions.memo: The clef fixes the pitches, so you know which note each line and space means.

questions.question: The treble clef is also known as the…
questions.memo: The treble clef curls around the line for G, so it is called the G clef.

questions.question: The bass clef is also known as the…
questions.memo: The bass clef's two dots sit around the line for F, so it is the F clef.

questions.question: Which clef is usually used for HIGHER (treble) pitches?
questions.memo: The treble clef is for higher voices and instruments; the bass clef for lower ones.

questions.question: The notes on the LINES of the treble clef, from bottom to top, spell…
questions.memo: Treble lines are E, G, B, D, F — remembered as 'Every Good Boy Deserves Fun'.

questions.question: The notes in the SPACES of the treble clef, from bottom to top, spell…
questions.memo: Treble spaces spell the word FACE, from bottom to top.

questions.question: The treble clef spaces spell the word ____.
questions.memo: Bottom to top, the treble clef spaces spell FACE.

questions.question: The notes on the LINES of the bass clef, from bottom to top, spell…
questions.memo: Bass lines are G, B, D, F, A — 'Good Boys Deserve Fun Always'.

questions.question: The notes in the SPACES of the bass clef, from bottom to top, spell…
questions.memo: Bass spaces are A, C, E, G — 'All Cows Eat Grass'.

questions.question: Music for higher instruments is usually written in the treble clef.
questions.memo: Treble clef suits higher pitches; bass clef suits lower ones.

questions.question: The musical alphabet uses the letters A to ____.
questions.memo: Music uses only seven letter names, A to G, then repeats.

questions.question: After the note G, the musical alphabet starts again at A.
questions.memo: The seven letters A–G repeat over and over as pitches rise.

questions.question: A helpful sentence for the treble clef LINES (E G B D F) is…
questions.memo: 'Every Good Boy Deserves Fun' gives the treble line notes E, G, B, D, F.

questions.question: Which note is named by the line the treble clef curls around?
questions.memo: The treble (G) clef curls around the second line from the bottom — the G line.

questions.question: Which note is named by the line between the bass clef's two dots?
questions.memo: The bass (F) clef's two dots sit on either side of the F line.

questions.question: The same letter names (A–G) are used in both the treble and bass clefs.
questions.memo: Both clefs use the same seven letters; only their position on the staff differs.

questions.question: A staff (or stave) is made of how many lines?
questions.memo: A staff has five lines and four spaces.

questions.question: The bass clef is also called the ____ clef.
questions.memo: The bass clef marks the F line, so it is the F clef.

questions.question: Sort each clue into the TREBLE clef or the BASS clef.
questions.expected: Treble = G clef / FACE; bass = F clef / All Cows Eat Grass.
questions.memo: Treble clef = G clef and FACE spaces; bass clef = F clef and ACEG spaces.

questions.question: Why do we need two different clefs?
options: So both high and low pitches fit neatly on a staff
To show how loud to play
questions.expected: So both high and low pitches fit neatly on a staff
questions.memo: Two clefs let very high and very low notes be written clearly without many extra lines.

CA.G7.MUL.A3.title: Beat and metre
CA.G7.MUL.A3.description: Music (CAPS G7) — Music literacy: Beat and metre.
CA.G7.MUL.A3.recovery_strategy: The metre is how the beats group — in 2s, 3s or 4s — and the first beat of each group is the strongest.

questions.question: What is the 'beat' in music?
options: The steady pulse you can tap or clap along to
questions.expected: The steady pulse you can tap or clap along to
questions.memo: The beat is the regular pulse — like a clock ticking — that you tap your foot to.

questions.question: What does 'metre' mean in music?
options: How the beats are grouped (in 2s, 3s or 4s)
questions.expected: How the beats are grouped (in 2s, 3s or 4s)
questions.memo: Metre is the grouping of beats into regular sets of 2, 3 or 4.

questions.question: Beats grouped in TWOS make which metre?
questions.memo: Duple metre groups beats in twos (strong-weak).

questions.question: Beats grouped in THREES make which metre?
questions.memo: Triple metre groups beats in threes — like a waltz (ONE-two-three).

questions.question: Beats grouped in FOURS make which metre?
questions.memo: Quadruple metre groups beats in fours, the most common metre in pop music.

questions.question: In every metre, the FIRST beat of the group is usually the strongest.
questions.memo: The first beat of each group is accented — it feels the strongest.

questions.question: A waltz, which goes 'ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three', is in which metre?
questions.memo: A waltz has three beats per group, so it is in triple metre.

questions.question: Beats grouped in twos are in ____ metre.
questions.memo: Two beats per group = duple metre.

questions.question: A march usually feels like ____ metre, with a strong LEFT-right, LEFT-right.
questions.memo: Marching naturally falls into two beats — duple metre.

questions.question: If you count '1-2-3-4, 1-2-3-4' steadily, the metre is…
questions.memo: Counting in fours is quadruple metre.

questions.question: Tempo and metre are exactly the same thing.
questions.memo: Tempo is the SPEED of the beat; metre is how the beats are GROUPED.

questions.question: The strong first beat of a group is called the…
questions.memo: An accent is extra stress; the first beat of each metre group is accented.

questions.question: Bars (or measures) on a staff are used to…
options: divide the music into equal groups of beats
questions.expected: divide the music into equal groups of beats
questions.memo: Bar-lines divide music into bars, each holding the same number of beats.

questions.question: A bar-line shows where one group of beats ends and the next begins.
questions.memo: Bar-lines separate the music into equal bars of beats.

questions.question: Which activity best helps you FEEL the beat?
options: Tapping your foot or clapping steadily
questions.expected: Tapping your foot or clapping steadily
questions.memo: Tapping or clapping along is the easiest way to feel the steady beat.

questions.question: The steady pulse of music is the ____.
questions.memo: The beat is the steady pulse underneath the music.

questions.question: Polyrhythm means…
options: two or more different rhythms played at the same time
questions.expected: two or more different rhythms played at the same time
questions.memo: Poly = many; a polyrhythm layers two or more rhythms together, common in African drumming.

questions.question: Clapping a rhythm of crotchets and quavers keeps the same steady beat underneath.
questions.memo: Rhythms can vary, but the steady beat (pulse) stays constant beneath them.

questions.question: Sort each example into its metre.
questions.expected: Marches and 1-2 counting are duple; waltzes and 1-2-3 counting are triple.
questions.memo: Group of two = duple; group of three = triple.

questions.question: Why is the beat important when playing in a group?
options: It keeps everyone together at the same pulse
It makes one person the loudest
questions.expected: It keeps everyone together at the same pulse
questions.memo: A shared steady beat lets a group stay together and play in time.

CA.G7.MUL.A4.title: Tonic sol-fa
CA.G7.MUL.A4.description: Music (CAPS G7) — Music literacy: Tonic sol-fa.
CA.G7.MUL.A4.recovery_strategy: Tonic sol-fa gives each note of the scale a name (doh re mi fa soh la ti doh) to help you sing it.

questions.question: What is tonic sol-fa used for?
options: Naming the notes of a scale to help you sing them
questions.expected: Naming the notes of a scale to help you sing them
questions.memo: Tonic sol-fa gives each scale note a singing name (doh, re, mi…) to help pitch it.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the tonic sol-fa names going UP?
options: doh re mi fa soh la ti doh
doh ti la soh fa mi re doh
mi fa soh la doh re ti
la ti doh re mi fa soh
questions.expected: doh re mi fa soh la ti doh
questions.memo: Going up the scale: doh re mi fa soh la ti doh.

questions.question: The 'home' note that the scale starts and ends on is called…
questions.memo: Doh is the tonic — the 'home' note the scale rests on.

questions.question: In tonic sol-fa the first note of the scale is ____.
questions.memo: Doh is the starting (home) note of the scale.

questions.question: Which sol-fa name comes directly AFTER 'mi' going up?
questions.memo: The order is mi, fa, soh — so fa follows mi.

questions.question: Which sol-fa name comes directly BEFORE 'doh' at the top of the scale?
questions.memo: Going up, ti leads to the top doh.

questions.question: 'Sight-singing' means singing music you are reading for the first time.
questions.memo: Sight-singing is reading and singing a melody at first sight, often using sol-fa.

questions.question: Tonic sol-fa can help you sing the right pitches without an instrument.
questions.memo: Sol-fa trains your ear so you can pitch the notes by their relationships.

questions.question: Going DOWN the scale, the order is…
options: doh ti la soh fa mi re doh
doh re mi fa soh la ti doh
questions.expected: doh ti la soh fa mi re doh
questions.memo: Coming down is the reverse: doh ti la soh fa mi re doh.

questions.question: The note 'soh' is the ____th note of the sol-fa scale (counting doh as 1).
questions.memo: doh(1) re(2) mi(3) fa(4) soh(5) — soh is the fifth note.

questions.question: Which sol-fa names are MISSING? doh, re, __, fa, __, la, ti
questions.memo: The full order is doh re mi fa soh la ti, so mi and soh fill the gaps.

questions.question: 'doh' at the bottom and 'doh' at the top of the scale are the same letter name an octave apart.
questions.memo: The scale starts and ends on doh, eight notes (an octave) apart.

questions.question: Tonic sol-fa is especially useful for…
questions.memo: Sol-fa is a singing tool, widely used in choirs to learn parts.

questions.question: Which note is the 'leading note' that pulls strongly up to doh?
questions.memo: Ti is the leading note — it sounds unfinished and 'leads' up to doh.

questions.question: Singing music you have never seen before, on sight, is called sight-____.
questions.memo: Sight-singing means singing at first sight.

questions.question: In tonic sol-fa, 'mi' is higher in pitch than 're'.
questions.memo: Going up the scale, each name is higher: re then mi.

questions.question: How many different sol-fa names are there in one octave of the major scale (not counting the repeated top doh)?
questions.memo: doh re mi fa soh la ti = seven names before doh repeats.

questions.question: Why do many singers learn a song in sol-fa first?
options: It helps them pitch the notes correctly
questions.expected: It helps them pitch the notes correctly
questions.memo: Sol-fa teaches the note relationships so singers hit the right pitches.

questions.question: Put the tonic sol-fa names in order going UP the scale.
questions.expected: doh, re, mi, fa, soh — the first five notes going up.
questions.memo: The scale rises doh re mi fa soh la ti doh.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about tonic sol-fa.

items.text: fa is the first note of the scale
sol-fa is used to choose how loud to sing

questions.expected: doh is home and ti leads to doh (true); fa is not first and sol-fa is not about volume (false).
questions.memo: Sol-fa names pitches; doh is home, ti leads to doh.

CA.G7.MUE.A1.title: Describing music
CA.G7.MUE.A1.description: Music (CAPS G7) — Listening & elements: Describing music.
CA.G7.MUE.A1.recovery_strategy: When you describe music, listen for how fast (tempo), how loud (dynamics), the beat grouping and the mood.

questions.question: In music, 'tempo' means…
options: how fast or slow the music is
how loud or soft it is
how high or low it is
questions.expected: how fast or slow the music is
questions.memo: Tempo is the speed of the beat — fast or slow.

questions.question: In music, 'dynamics' means…
options: how loud or soft the music is
questions.expected: how loud or soft the music is
questions.memo: Dynamics describe volume — loud (forte) to soft (piano).

questions.question: If music is played very SOFTLY, its dynamics are…
questions.memo: Soft playing is described as piano; loud is forte.

questions.question: If music gradually gets FASTER, its tempo is…
questions.memo: A change in tempo means the speed changes — here, getting faster.

questions.question: 'Texture' in music describes how many layers of sound are playing together.
questions.memo: Texture is thin (few sounds) or thick (many layers playing at once).

questions.question: A solo singer with one quiet guitar would have a __ texture.
questions.memo: Few layers = thin texture; a full band or choir = thick texture.

questions.question: Which word describes the MOOD a piece of music creates?
questions.memo: Mood is the feeling the music gives — happy, sad, calm, exciting, and so on.

questions.question: The speed of the music is called the ____.
questions.memo: Tempo = speed.

questions.question: How loud or soft music is, is called its ____.
questions.memo: Dynamics = volume (loudness).

questions.question: Slow, soft music in a minor key often creates which mood?
questions.memo: Slow, soft, minor music usually feels sad, gentle or calm.

questions.question: Fast, loud music with strong drums often creates which mood?
questions.memo: Fast, loud, driving music usually feels exciting and energetic.

questions.question: You can describe a piece of music by its tempo, dynamics, metre and mood.
questions.memo: These are key elements used to describe and compare music.

questions.question: 'Forte' is a music word meaning…
questions.memo: Forte means loud; piano means soft.

questions.question: Lyrics are…
questions.memo: Lyrics are the words of a song.

questions.question: Listening for the STORY or message of a song means paying attention to its lyrics.
questions.memo: The lyrics often carry the story or message of a song.

questions.question: A 'graphic score' or sound picture is…
options: a drawing that shows the sounds in a piece of music
questions.expected: a drawing that shows the sounds in a piece of music
questions.memo: A graphic score uses pictures or shapes (not notes) to show sounds, like a rising line for a rising pitch.

questions.question: When music changes from soft to loud, we say the __ have changed.
questions.memo: A change from soft to loud is a change in dynamics.

questions.question: Sort each describing word under TEMPO or DYNAMICS.
questions.expected: Fast and slow describe tempo; loud and soft describe dynamics.
questions.memo: Tempo = speed (fast/slow); dynamics = volume (loud/soft).

questions.question: Why is it useful to describe music using these elements?
options: It helps you compare pieces and explain how they make you feel
questions.expected: It helps you compare pieces and explain how they make you feel
questions.memo: Describing tempo, dynamics, texture and mood lets you talk about and compare music.

questions.question: 'Texture' contrast in music is heard when the music changes from…
questions.memo: A change from a thin to a thick texture (one voice to many) is a texture contrast.

CA.G7.MUE.A2.title: Instruments in a performance
CA.G7.MUE.A2.description: Music (CAPS G7) — Listening & elements: Instruments in a performance.
CA.G7.MUE.A2.recovery_strategy: Each instrument has its own sound; with practice you can pick out a drum, guitar or flute by ear.

questions.question: Which of these is a STRING instrument?
questions.memo: A guitar makes sound from vibrating strings, so it is a string instrument.

questions.question: Which of these is a WIND instrument (you blow it)?
questions.memo: A flute is played by blowing air, making it a wind instrument.

questions.question: Which of these is a PERCUSSION instrument (you hit or shake it)?
questions.memo: A drum is struck, so it belongs to the percussion family.

questions.question: The piano makes its sound when…
options: small hammers strike strings inside it
questions.expected: small hammers strike strings inside it
questions.memo: Pressing a piano key makes a hammer strike a string inside.

questions.question: A trumpet is played by blowing air through it.
questions.memo: A trumpet is a brass wind instrument — you blow (buzz your lips) into it.

questions.question: A marimba and a xylophone are mainly which type of instrument?
questions.memo: You strike marimba and xylophone bars with beaters, so they are percussion.

questions.question: Which instrument would you most likely hear keeping the BEAT in a band?
questions.memo: Drums and other percussion usually keep the steady beat in a band.

questions.question: An instrument you blow into is a ____ instrument.
questions.memo: Wind instruments are sounded by blowing air.

questions.question: An instrument with strings you pluck or bow is a ____ instrument.
questions.memo: String instruments sound from vibrating strings.

questions.question: Which of these is a traditional South African instrument?
questions.memo: African drums like the djembe are traditional percussion instruments.

questions.question: Listening carefully helps you pick out which instruments are playing.
questions.memo: Active listening lets you identify instruments by their distinct sounds.

questions.question: The human VOICE used to make music counts as…
questions.memo: The voice is treated as an instrument — the oldest and most natural one.

questions.question: A violin makes its sound mainly when the player…
options: draws a bow across the strings
questions.expected: draws a bow across the strings
questions.memo: A violin is bowed (or plucked) — its strings vibrate to make sound.

questions.question: A guitar and a violin both make sound from vibrating strings.
questions.memo: Both are string instruments, sounded by vibrating strings.

questions.question: 'Body percussion' means making rhythmic sounds by…
options: clapping, clicking, stamping or patting yourself
questions.expected: clapping, clicking, stamping or patting yourself
questions.memo: Body percussion uses your own body — clapping, stamping, clicking — as the instrument.

questions.question: Which group of instruments would you find in a marching band?
questions.memo: Marching bands feature loud brass and percussion that carry outdoors.

questions.question: A drum, shaker or tambourine belongs to the ____ family.
questions.memo: Instruments you hit or shake are percussion.

questions.question: Sort each instrument into its family.
questions.expected: Guitar and violin are strings; flute is wind; drum is percussion.
questions.memo: Strings vibrate, wind is blown, percussion is hit or shaken.

questions.question: Why does identifying instruments help you enjoy a performance?
options: You hear how different sounds blend to make the music
questions.expected: You hear how different sounds blend to make the music
questions.memo: Recognising instruments deepens your listening and appreciation of how music is built.

questions.question: A brass instrument you might hear in a band is the…
questions.memo: The trumpet is a brass wind instrument common in bands.

CA.G7.MUP.A1.title: Creating music
CA.G7.MUP.A1.description: Music (CAPS G7) — Performing & creating: Creating music.
CA.G7.MUP.A1.recovery_strategy: An ostinato or riff is a short pattern repeated; question-and-answer is one phrase 'answered' by another.

questions.question: An 'ostinato' is…
options: a short pattern repeated over and over
questions.expected: a short pattern repeated over and over
questions.memo: An ostinato is a short rhythmic or melodic pattern repeated throughout a piece.

questions.question: A 'riff' in popular music is…
questions.memo: A riff is a short, catchy musical pattern that repeats, often on guitar or keyboard.

questions.question: In 'question and answer' (call and response), the second phrase…
options: responds to the first, like an answer
questions.expected: responds to the first, like an answer
questions.memo: Question-and-answer pairs a 'question' phrase with an 'answer' phrase that responds to it.

questions.question: Repeating a pattern (repetition) is one way to build a piece of music.
questions.memo: Repetition gives music shape and makes patterns memorable.

questions.question: A 'graphic score' creates music using…
options: pictures, shapes or symbols instead of normal notes
questions.expected: pictures, shapes or symbols instead of normal notes
questions.memo: A graphic score uses drawings and symbols to show sounds — non-conventional notation.

questions.question: A short pattern repeated again and again is called an ____.
questions.memo: An ostinato is a repeated short pattern.

questions.question: Improvising means…
options: making up music on the spot
copying a recording note for note
questions.expected: making up music on the spot
questions.memo: Improvising is creating music in the moment, without writing it down first.

questions.question: You can improvise a rhythm by clapping or drumming a pattern over a steady beat.
questions.memo: Rhythmic improvisation means making up rhythms over an ostinato or steady beat.

questions.question: 'Melodic' question and answer uses…
questions.memo: Melodic Q&A uses pitched tunes; rhythmic Q&A uses rhythms only.

questions.question: Which is the BEST description of composing?
options: Creating your own music and being able to keep it
questions.expected: Creating your own music and being able to keep it
questions.memo: Composing is creating original music, often written or recorded so it can be repeated.

questions.question: A riff and an ostinato are both built on repetition.
questions.memo: Both rely on repeating a short pattern.

questions.question: Drumming a repeating pattern on African drums while others improvise over it is using an…
questions.memo: The repeating drum pattern is an ostinato that others improvise over.

questions.question: Making up music on the spot is called ____.
questions.memo: Improvising = making up music in the moment.

questions.question: A sound picture of a storm might use which idea?
options: Soft shakers growing to loud crashing drums
questions.expected: Soft shakers growing to loud crashing drums
questions.memo: A sound picture matches sounds to a story — rising dynamics paint a building storm.

questions.question: Non-conventional notation, like a graphic score, can show sounds without using staff notes.
questions.memo: Graphic scores use shapes and symbols instead of standard notes.

questions.question: Which pair is 'question and answer'?
options: One phrase that sounds unfinished, then one that completes it
questions.expected: One phrase that sounds unfinished, then one that completes it
questions.memo: The 'question' sounds open; the 'answer' resolves and completes it.

questions.question: Why is repetition useful when creating music?
options: It makes patterns easy to remember and hold a piece together
questions.expected: It makes patterns easy to remember and hold a piece together
questions.memo: Repeated patterns are memorable and give a piece unity and structure.

questions.question: Body percussion can be used to perform a rhythmic ostinato.
questions.memo: Clapping or stamping a repeated pattern is a body-percussion ostinato.

questions.question: Sort each idea as a way of CREATING music or NOT.

items.text: Improvising a rhythm over a beat

questions.expected: Improvising and using an ostinato create music; reading covers and choosing poster colours do not.
questions.memo: Creating music means making sound patterns — improvising, repeating, composing.

questions.question: Put these steps for making a simple class composition in a sensible order.

items.text: Choose a steady beat or ostinato
Add a repeated riff or pattern
Improvise a question-and-answer over the top

questions.expected: Start with a beat/ostinato, add a riff, improvise Q&A, then perform.
questions.memo: Build from a steady foundation up to the finished performance.

CA.G7.MUP.A2.title: Singing and song types
CA.G7.MUP.A2.description: Music (CAPS G7) — Performing & creating: Singing and song types.
CA.G7.MUP.A2.recovery_strategy: A round is a song where groups start at different times; body percussion is clapping, clicking or stamping a beat.

questions.question: Singing 'in tune' means…
questions.memo: Singing in tune means matching the correct pitches accurately.

questions.question: A 'round' is a song where…
options: groups sing the same tune but start at different times
questions.expected: groups sing the same tune but start at different times

questions.question: A 'folk song' is usually…

questions.question: Part-singing means different groups sing different musical parts at the same time.

questions.question: A 'descant' is…

questions.question: Which is a benefit of singing together in a group?

You sing as fast as possible

questions.question: A traditional song passed down through a culture is a ____ song.
questions.memo: Folk songs are traditional and handed down over time.

questions.question: Indigenous and cultural songs are examples of folk songs.

questions.question: To sing a round successfully, each group must…

questions.question: 'Light music' usually means…

questions.question: Singing in tune improves with regular practice and careful listening.
questions.memo: Like any skill, accurate singing improves with practice and listening to your pitch.

questions.question: African drumming often accompanies singing by providing…
options: a strong rhythmic beat and ostinato patterns

questions.question: Why do we warm up the voice before singing?

questions.question: A higher decorative part sung above the main tune is a ____.
questions.memo: A descant floats above the main melody.

Traditional song passed down in a culture
Often sung by ear over generations

questions.question: Why is singing the National Anthem an important shared experience?
options: It brings people together across languages and cultures
questions.expected: It brings people together across languages and cultures
questions.memo: The anthem unites people across South Africa's languages and cultures.

CA.G7.VAE.A1.title: Art elements
CA.G7.VAE.A1.description: Visual Arts (CAPS G7) — Art elements & design: Art elements.
CA.G7.VAE.A1.recovery_strategy: The art elements are the basic 'ingredients' of any artwork: line, shape, tone, texture and colour.

questions.question: The 'art elements' are…
options: the basic building blocks of any artwork
the rules for hanging a painting
questions.expected: the basic building blocks of any artwork
questions.memo: Art elements — line, shape, tone, texture, colour — are the basic ingredients of art.

questions.question: Which of these is an art element?
questions.memo: Line is one of the visual art elements; loudness and tempo belong to music.

questions.question: 'Texture' in art means…
options: how a surface looks or feels (rough or smooth)
questions.expected: how a surface looks or feels (rough or smooth)
questions.memo: Texture is the surface quality — rough, smooth, bumpy — real or implied.

questions.question: 'Tone' (or value) in art means…
options: how light or dark something is
questions.expected: how light or dark something is
questions.memo: Tone is the lightness or darkness of an area, from white through greys to black.

questions.question: A 'shape' is…
options: a flat, enclosed area such as a circle or square
questions.expected: a flat, enclosed area such as a circle or square
questions.memo: A shape is a 2D enclosed area, like a circle, square or organic blob.

questions.question: Line, shape, tone, texture and colour are all art elements.
questions.memo: These five are core visual art elements.

questions.question: How light or dark something is, is called ____.
questions.memo: Tone (value) describes lightness and darkness.

questions.question: The surface quality of an artwork — rough or smooth — is its ____.
questions.memo: Texture is the surface feel or look.

questions.question: Which element would an artist use to show the OUTLINE of an object?
questions.memo: A line traces edges and outlines.

questions.question: Shading a drawing from dark to light shows which element?
questions.memo: Shading creates tone — a range from dark to light.

questions.question: Texture can be REAL (you can feel it) or IMPLIED (it only looks rough).
questions.memo: Real texture is felt; implied texture is created with marks to look rough or smooth.

questions.question: A drawing made only of dots and small marks is using which technique?
questions.memo: Mark-making uses dots, dashes and marks to build tone and texture.

questions.question: Which pair are BOTH art elements?
questions.memo: Colour and line are both visual elements; tempo, rhythm and lyrics belong to music.

questions.question: A circle and a square are examples of shapes.
questions.memo: Both are enclosed 2D shapes.

questions.question: 'Organic' shapes are…
options: free, natural shapes like leaves or clouds
questions.expected: free, natural shapes like leaves or clouds
questions.memo: Organic shapes are irregular and natural; geometric shapes are regular like circles and squares.

questions.question: Which element creates the feeling of ROUGHNESS in a picture?
questions.memo: Texture conveys rough or smooth surfaces.

questions.question: A flat enclosed area such as a triangle is a ____.
questions.memo: An enclosed flat area is a shape.

questions.question: Artists can combine several art elements in one artwork.
questions.memo: Most artworks use many elements together — line, shape, tone, texture and colour.

questions.question: Sort each word into ART ELEMENT or NOT an art element.
questions.expected: Line and texture are art elements; tempo and loudness are music words.
questions.memo: Visual art elements: line, shape, tone, texture, colour. Tempo/loudness are musical.

questions.question: Why are the art elements useful to know?
options: They give you a language to describe and create art
questions.expected: They give you a language to describe and create art
questions.memo: Knowing the elements lets you talk about, plan and make artworks.

CA.G7.VAE.A2.title: Colour theory
CA.G7.VAE.A2.description: Visual Arts (CAPS G7) — Art elements & design: Colour theory.
CA.G7.VAE.A2.recovery_strategy: Complementary colours sit opposite on the colour wheel; monochromatic means tints and shades of one colour.

questions.question: The three PRIMARY colours are…
questions.memo: Primary colours — red, yellow, blue — cannot be mixed from other colours.

questions.question: Mixing two primary colours makes a…
questions.memo: Secondary colours (green, orange, purple) come from mixing two primaries.

questions.question: Blue + yellow makes…
questions.memo: Blue mixed with yellow makes green.

questions.question: Red + yellow makes…
questions.memo: Red mixed with yellow makes orange.

questions.question: 'Complementary' colours are colours that…
options: sit opposite each other on the colour wheel
are right next to each other
questions.expected: sit opposite each other on the colour wheel
questions.memo: Complementary colours are opposites on the wheel, like red and green, and contrast strongly.

questions.question: 'Monochromatic' colour means using…
options: different tints and shades of ONE colour
questions.expected: different tints and shades of ONE colour
questions.memo: Monochromatic = one colour in many lightnesses (tints and shades).

questions.question: Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel are ____ colours.
questions.memo: Opposites on the wheel are complementary.

questions.question: Using only shades of blue is an example of a ____ colour scheme.
questions.memo: One colour in many shades = monochromatic.

questions.question: Adding WHITE to a colour makes a…
questions.memo: White makes a tint (lighter); black makes a shade (darker).

questions.question: Adding BLACK to a colour makes a…
questions.memo: Black darkens a colour into a shade.

questions.question: Red and green are a pair of complementary colours.
questions.memo: Red and green sit opposite on the wheel — a complementary pair.

questions.question: Which colours are SECONDARY colours?
questions.memo: Green, orange and purple are made by mixing primaries.

questions.question: Blue + red makes…
questions.memo: Blue mixed with red makes purple (violet).

questions.question: You can mix any colour you need from the three primary colours plus white and black.
questions.memo: Primaries plus white and black let you mix a huge range of colours.

questions.question: Warm colours (reds, oranges, yellows) often feel…
questions.memo: Warm colours feel energetic and cosy; cool colours feel calm.

questions.question: Cool colours (blues, greens) often feel…
questions.memo: Cool colours tend to feel calm and restful.

questions.question: Adding white to red makes the tint we call ____.
questions.memo: Red + white = pink, a tint of red.

questions.question: Sort each colour into PRIMARY or SECONDARY.
questions.expected: Red and blue are primary; green and orange are secondary (mixed).
questions.memo: Primaries: red, yellow, blue. Secondaries (mixed): green, orange, purple.

questions.question: Why might an artist choose complementary colours?
options: To create strong contrast that makes each colour stand out
To make the picture look grey
questions.expected: To create strong contrast that makes each colour stand out
questions.memo: Complementary pairs contrast strongly and make each colour appear more vivid.

questions.question: Orange is a secondary colour made from red and yellow.
questions.memo: Red mixed with yellow makes the secondary colour orange.

CA.G7.VAE.A3.title: Design principles
CA.G7.VAE.A3.description: Visual Arts (CAPS G7) — Art elements & design: Design principles.
CA.G7.VAE.A3.recovery_strategy: Design principles are the 'rules' for arranging elements: balance, contrast, pattern, proportion and emphasis.

questions.question: Design principles are…
options: ways of arranging the art elements in an artwork
questions.expected: ways of arranging the art elements in an artwork
questions.memo: Design principles are 'rules' for arranging elements: balance, contrast, pattern, proportion, emphasis.

questions.question: 'Balance' in design means…
options: the visual weight is spread evenly
questions.expected: the visual weight is spread evenly
questions.memo: Balance is the even distribution of visual weight so an artwork feels stable.

questions.question: 'Contrast' in design means…
questions.memo: Contrast sets different elements side by side — light/dark, big/small — to create interest.

questions.question: 'Pattern' is…
questions.memo: A pattern is a motif repeated in a regular way.

questions.question: 'Proportion' is about…
options: the size of parts compared to each other
questions.expected: the size of parts compared to each other
questions.memo: Proportion is the relative size of parts of an artwork to each other and the whole.

questions.question: 'Emphasis' (a focal point) means…
options: drawing attention to the most important part
questions.expected: drawing attention to the most important part
questions.memo: Emphasis creates a focal point that the eye is drawn to first.

questions.question: Repeating a shape across a surface creates pattern.
questions.memo: Regular repetition of a motif makes a pattern.

questions.question: Spreading visual weight evenly in an artwork is called ____.
questions.memo: Even visual weight = balance.

questions.question: Placing a small bright object among large dull ones creates ____.
questions.memo: Differences in size and colour create contrast.

questions.question: An artist makes one flower bright red while the rest are grey. This uses…
questions.memo: The single bright flower becomes the focal point — emphasis.

questions.question: Design principles and art elements are the same thing.
questions.memo: Elements are the ingredients (line, colour…); principles are how you ARRANGE them.

questions.question: Symmetrical balance means…
options: both sides look the same or mirror each other
questions.expected: both sides look the same or mirror each other
questions.memo: Symmetrical balance mirrors one side with the other.

questions.question: A repeated zig-zag border around a plate is an example of…
questions.memo: A repeated motif like a zig-zag border is a pattern.

questions.question: Good proportion helps the parts of an artwork look right together.
questions.memo: Proportion keeps the sizes of parts believable and pleasing.

questions.question: Which principle helps stop an artwork looking lop-sided?
questions.memo: Balance distributes weight so the work doesn't feel lop-sided.

questions.question: Which principle is mainly about REPETITION?
questions.memo: Pattern is built from regular repetition.

questions.question: The part of an artwork your eye is drawn to first is the ____ point.
questions.memo: The focal point is created by emphasis.

questions.question: Match each description to its design principle.

items.text: Both sides have equal visual weight
A dark shape next to a light one

questions.expected: Equal weight and mirror images = balance; dark next to light = contrast; repeated motif = pattern.
questions.memo: Balance spreads weight; contrast pairs opposites; pattern repeats a motif.

questions.question: Why do artists use design principles?
options: To arrange elements so the artwork is clear and pleasing
questions.expected: To arrange elements so the artwork is clear and pleasing
questions.memo: Principles guide how elements are arranged so the work communicates well.

questions.question: Repeating the same motif in regular rows is an example of which principle?
questions.memo: Regular repetition of a motif creates pattern.

CA.G7.VAM.A1.title: Drawing and 2D media

questions.memo: Art media are the materials and tools — pencil, charcoal, paint, ink, and so on.

options: the different marks (dots, lines, dashes) used to build a drawing
questions.expected: the different marks (dots, lines, dashes) used to build a drawing

questions.question: 'Colour-mixing' in painting means…
options: combining paints to make new colours
questions.expected: combining paints to make new colours
questions.memo: Colour-mixing blends paints to create the colours you need.

questions.question: 'Brush manipulation' refers to…
options: the different ways you can move and use a brush
questions.expected: the different ways you can move and use a brush
questions.memo: Brush manipulation is controlling the brush — strokes, pressure, angle — for different effects.

questions.question: Simple etching with a scraperboard works by…
options: scratching through a dark surface to reveal a light layer beneath

questions.question: Different drawing tools (pencil, charcoal, pen) make different kinds of marks.
questions.memo: Each medium has its own qualities and mark range.

questions.question: The materials an artist works with, like paint and charcoal, are called ____.
questions.memo: Media are the art materials.

questions.question: 'Lettering' in design is…
options: drawing letters and words as part of an artwork
questions.expected: drawing letters and words as part of an artwork
questions.memo: Lettering is designing letters and text, often combining images and words.

questions.question: 'Pattern-making' in 2D art means…
options: repeating shapes or motifs to decorate a surface
questions.expected: repeating shapes or motifs to decorate a surface
questions.memo: Pattern-making repeats motifs across a surface as decoration.

questions.question: Texture in a drawing can be created with mark-making, like cross-hatching.
questions.memo: Hatching and cross-hatching are mark-making methods that build texture and tone.

questions.question: Cross-hatching is…
options: sets of crossing lines used to build tone
questions.expected: sets of crossing lines used to build tone
questions.memo: Cross-hatching layers crossing lines to darken and texture an area.

questions.question: Which tool would give the SOFTEST, smudgiest marks?
questions.memo: Charcoal smudges and gives soft, dark marks; a hard pencil and pen give crisp lines.

questions.question: Combining images and text is a common part of lettering and design projects.
questions.memo: Lettering projects often blend images and words together.

questions.question: Exploring 'a variety of media' means an artist…
options: tries different materials to see their effects
questions.expected: tries different materials to see their effects
questions.memo: Exploring media means experimenting with many materials and techniques.

questions.question: Crossing sets of lines to build up tone is called cross-____.
questions.memo: Cross-hatching builds tone with crossing lines.

questions.question: Personal interpretation means an artist shows their OWN view of a subject, not just a copy.
questions.memo: Personal interpretation adds the artist's own ideas and feelings, beyond mere copying.

questions.question: Why do artists practise different 2D techniques?
options: To widen the range of effects and ideas they can express
questions.expected: To widen the range of effects and ideas they can express
questions.memo: Practising techniques expands what an artist can express.

questions.question: Layering crossing lines to darken an area in a drawing is called…
questions.memo: Cross-hatching builds tone and texture with crossing lines.

CA.G7.VAM.A2.title: Making in 3D
CA.G7.VAM.A2.description: Visual Arts (CAPS G7) — Making in 2D & 3D: Making in 3D.

questions.question: A '3D' (three-dimensional) artwork is one that…
options: has height, width AND depth — you can walk around it
questions.expected: has height, width AND depth — you can walk around it
questions.memo: 3D works are solid — they have depth as well as height and width, like a sculpture.

questions.question: 'Construction' in 3D art means…
options: joining materials together to build a form
questions.expected: joining materials together to build a form
questions.memo: Construction builds a 3D form by joining materials.

questions.question: 'Modelling' in 3D art usually means…
options: shaping a soft material like clay
questions.expected: shaping a soft material like clay
questions.memo: Modelling shapes a malleable material such as clay into a form.

questions.question: 'Spatial awareness' means understanding…
options: how forms sit in space and relate to each other
questions.expected: how forms sit in space and relate to each other
questions.memo: Spatial awareness is sensing depth, space and how parts relate in three dimensions.

questions.question: Showing depth on a flat surface so things look near or far uses…

questions.question: Using RECYCLABLE materials in art shows…

questions.question: An artwork with height, width and depth is ____.

questions.question: Making forms look near or far on a flat surface uses ____.

questions.question: A drawing on paper is a 3D artwork.

questions.question: Which material is best suited to MODELLING?
questions.memo: Soft, mouldable clay is ideal for modelling a 3D form.

questions.question: Which is an example of using recyclable materials in art?
options: Building a sculpture from cardboard boxes and bottle tops
questions.expected: Building a sculpture from cardboard boxes and bottle tops
questions.memo: Found and recyclable materials like boxes and bottle tops can be reused for sculpture.

questions.question: 'Plane' and 'depth' are ideas that help an artist think about 3D space.
questions.memo: Understanding planes and depth develops spatial awareness in 3D work.

questions.question: Why warm up an idea with sketches before making a 3D work?
options: To plan the form before building it
questions.expected: To plan the form before building it
questions.memo: Planning sketches help work out the form before committing materials.

questions.question: A sculpture you can view from ALL sides is described as…

questions.question: Caring for your tools and cleaning up is part of good craftsmanship.

questions.question: Sort each item into 2D or 3D.

questions.question: Why is spatial awareness important in 3D art?

questions.expected: It helps you judge form, depth and how parts fit in space
questions.memo: Spatial awareness lets you build believable, well-proportioned 3D forms.

questions.question: A clay sculpture you can view from every side is a 3D artwork.

CA.G7.VAL.A1.title: Looking and analysing

questions.question: 'Visual literacy' means being able to…

questions.expected: look at, understand and talk about images and artworks
questions.memo: Visual literacy is 'reading' images — understanding and discussing what you see.

questions.question: To analyse an artwork, you should first…
options: look carefully and describe what you see
questions.expected: look carefully and describe what you see
questions.memo: Analysis begins with careful looking and describing the elements you notice.

questions.memo: A still life depicts arranged inanimate objects.

questions.question: A traditional MASK in many cultures can be used for…

questions.question: An image that stands for an idea, like a dove for peace, is a ____.
questions.memo: A symbol represents an idea visually.

questions.question: When you 'interpret' an artwork, you…
options: work out what it might mean or express
questions.expected: work out what it might mean or express
questions.memo: Interpreting means making sense of the meaning or message of an artwork.

questions.question: Looking at a painting of a building, an artist might notice its…

questions.question: Different people can interpret the same artwork in different ways.

questions.question: 'Groups of figures' in an artwork are…

questions.question: Which question helps you ANALYSE an artwork?

How much did the frame cost?

questions.memo: Good analysis asks what you see and what it might mean.

questions.question: Talking and writing about art helps you understand it more deeply.
questions.memo: Expressing your observations in words deepens your understanding.

questions.question: A red colour in an artwork might SYMBOLISE…
options: love, danger or energy depending on context
questions.expected: love, danger or energy depending on context
questions.memo: Colours carry symbolic meaning that depends on context — red can mean love, danger or energy.

questions.question: 'Local craft' refers to…

questions.expected: hand-made objects from a community, like beadwork or pottery
questions.memo: Local craft is hand-made work by community crafters — beadwork, weaving, pottery.

questions.question: An arrangement of objects like fruit and a jug is a ____ life.

CA.G7.VAL.A2.title: The artist and research
