questions.memo: A sketchbook records and develops ideas and references for projects.

questions.question: An artist who shows everyday life in their community is acting as an…
questions.memo: Depicting community life is the artist observing and reflecting society.

questions.question: Researching other artists' work can give you ideas for your own.
questions.memo: Studying other artists is a valuable source of inspiration and technique.

questions.question: Someone who designs logos, posters and layouts is a graphic ____.
questions.memo: A graphic designer creates visual communication like logos and posters.

questions.question: Why is it useful to know that art has many careers?
options: It shows art skills can lead to real, paying work
questions.expected: It shows art skills can lead to real, paying work
questions.memo: Knowing the careers shows art is a real pathway to work.

questions.question: Reliable research sources for an art project include…
questions.memo: Books, galleries, museums and reliable sites are good research sources.

questions.question: An artist can both contribute to AND observe their society.
questions.memo: Artists do both — they add to culture and reflect the world they observe.

questions.question: Preliminary sketches are…
options: early rough drawings to plan a final work
questions.expected: early rough drawings to plan a final work
questions.memo: Preliminary sketches explore and plan ideas before the final artwork.

questions.question: Early rough drawings made to plan an artwork are called ____ sketches.
questions.memo: Preliminary (rough, planning) sketches come before the final work.

questions.question: Sort each task into RESEARCH or MAKING.
questions.expected: Collecting references and reading are research; shading and mixing paint are making.
questions.memo: Research gathers ideas; making produces the artwork.

questions.question: Put the steps of starting an art project in a sensible order.
questions.expected: Choose a theme, research, sketch ideas, then make the final work.
questions.memo: Plan before you make: theme → research → sketches → final piece.

CA.G8.MUL.A1.title: Duration and metre
CA.G8.MUL.A1.description: Music (CAPS G8) — Music literacy: Duration and metre.
CA.G8.MUL.A1.recovery_strategy: The top number of a time signature counts beats in a bar; 6/8 groups six quavers into two main beats.

questions.question: A 'time signature' at the start of music tells you…
options: how many beats are in each bar and what kind of beat
questions.expected: how many beats are in each bar and what kind of beat
questions.memo: The time signature gives the number of beats per bar (top) and the beat value (bottom).

questions.question: In the time signature 4/4, the top number means…
questions.memo: The top '4' means four beats fill each bar.

questions.question: In 3/4 time, how many crotchet beats are in a bar?
questions.memo: 3/4 means three crotchet beats per bar — waltz time.

questions.question: In 2/4 time, how many crotchet beats are in a bar?
questions.memo: 2/4 means two crotchet beats per bar — march feel.

questions.question: The bottom '4' in 4/4 tells you the beat is counted in…
questions.memo: A bottom 4 means the beat is a crotchet (quarter note).

questions.question: 6/8 is a 'compound duple' time. It has two MAIN beats, each divided into…
questions.memo: 6/8 groups six quavers into two main beats of three quavers each — a swaying compound feel.

questions.question: In 6/8 time there are six quavers in each bar.
questions.memo: 6/8 has six quavers per bar, felt as two groups of three.

questions.question: The top number of a time signature shows the number of ____ in a bar.
questions.memo: The top number counts the beats per bar.

questions.question: Which time signature is a waltz usually in?
questions.memo: A waltz is in 3/4 — three beats per bar.

questions.question: Which time signature is most common in pop and rock music?
questions.memo: 4/4 (common time) is the most widely used metre in pop and rock.

questions.question: 4/4 time is sometimes called 'common time'.
questions.memo: 4/4 is so widespread it is nicknamed common time.

questions.question: How many crotchet beats fit in a bar of 2/4 plus a bar of 3/4?
questions.memo: 2 beats + 3 beats = 5 crotchet beats in total.

questions.question: Reading rhythm correctly means clapping the notes while keeping…
options: a steady beat in the right time signature
questions.expected: a steady beat in the right time signature
questions.memo: You clap the rhythm against a steady beat in the bar's time signature.

questions.question: A 'compound duple' time signature you study in Grade 8 is ____.
questions.memo: 6/8 is the compound duple metre.

questions.question: In 3/4 time, three minims fit in one bar.
questions.memo: 3/4 holds three CROTCHET beats; three minims would be six beats, too many.

questions.question: A bar of 4/4 could be filled by…
questions.memo: A semibreve is four beats, exactly filling a 4/4 bar.

questions.question: The time signature stays the same unless the music shows a new one.
questions.memo: A time signature holds until a new one is written.

questions.question: Sort each time signature by how many crotchet beats are in a bar.
questions.expected: 2/4 = 2 beats, 3/4 = 3 beats, 4/4 and common time = 4 beats.
questions.memo: The top number gives the beats per bar; common time is 4/4.

questions.question: Why does music need a time signature?
options: So players know how to group and count the beats
questions.expected: So players know how to group and count the beats
questions.memo: The time signature tells everyone how to count and feel the metre.

questions.question: In 4/4 time, two minims fill…
questions.memo: Two minims = four beats = one full bar of 4/4.

CA.G8.MUL.A2.title: Major scales
CA.G8.MUL.A2.description: Music (CAPS G8) — Music literacy: Major scales.
CA.G8.MUL.A2.recovery_strategy: A major scale follows the pattern tone-tone-semitone-tone-tone-tone-semitone from its starting note.

questions.question: A 'scale' is…
options: a set of notes in order, going up or down by step
questions.expected: a set of notes in order, going up or down by step
questions.memo: A scale is a ladder of notes in order, stepping up or down.

questions.question: How many different notes are in one octave of a major scale (before it repeats)?
questions.memo: A major scale has seven different notes, then the eighth repeats the first an octave higher.

questions.question: The pattern of a major scale is…
questions.memo: Every major scale follows T-T-S-T-T-T-S.

questions.question: A 'semitone' is…
options: the smallest step between two notes (e.g. E to F)
questions.expected: the smallest step between two notes (e.g. E to F)
questions.memo: A semitone is the smallest step, like E–F or B–C, or any note to the next key.

questions.question: A 'tone' (whole tone) is…
questions.memo: A tone is two semitones — a whole step.

questions.question: Which major scale has NO sharps or flats?
questions.memo: C major uses only the white keys — no sharps or flats.

questions.question: Which note is sharp in G major?
questions.memo: G major has one sharp: F#.

questions.question: Which one flat does F major use?
questions.memo: F major has one flat: B flat.

questions.question: How many sharps does D major have?
questions.memo: D major has two sharps: F# and C#.

questions.question: A major scale starts and ends on the same letter name, called the ____.
questions.memo: The tonic is the home note the scale is named after.

questions.question: Every major scale uses the same pattern of tones and semitones.
questions.memo: All major scales share the T-T-S-T-T-T-S pattern, just starting on different notes.

questions.question: Between which two notes in C major is there a SEMITONE?
questions.memo: In C major the semitones fall between E–F and B–C.

questions.question: The smallest step between two notes is a ____.
questions.memo: A semitone is the smallest step.

questions.question: The C major scale, going up, is…
options: C D E F G A B C
C B A G F E D C
questions.expected: C D E F G A B C
questions.memo: C major ascends C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C using only white keys.

questions.question: G major and C major both contain the note B natural.
questions.memo: G major's sharp is F#, not B, so B stays natural — as in C major.

questions.question: Why do different major scales need sharps or flats?
options: To keep the same tone-semitone pattern from a new starting note
questions.expected: To keep the same tone-semitone pattern from a new starting note
questions.memo: Sharps/flats keep the major pattern intact when you start on a different note.

questions.question: Which scale uses the note F#?
questions.memo: G major contains F#; C major and F major do not.

questions.question: Sort each major scale by how many sharps or flats it has.
questions.expected: C major = none; G and D major = sharps; F major = one flat.
questions.memo: C none, G one sharp, D two sharps, F one flat.

questions.question: Put the notes of the C major scale in order going UP from C.
questions.expected: C, D, E, F, G — the first five notes of C major.
questions.memo: C major steps up C D E F G A B C.

questions.question: Every major scale uses the pattern tone-tone-semitone-tone-tone-tone-semitone.
questions.memo: All major scales share the same tone/semitone pattern from their starting note.

CA.G8.MUL.A3.title: Reading in keys
CA.G8.MUL.A3.description: Music (CAPS G8) — Music literacy: Reading in keys.
CA.G8.MUL.A3.recovery_strategy: The key tells you which sharps or flats to use throughout the piece.

questions.question: The 'key' of a piece tells you…
options: which scale and notes the music is mainly built from
questions.expected: which scale and notes the music is mainly built from
questions.memo: The key names the main scale (and its sharps/flats) the music uses.

questions.question: If a piece is in G major, which note will usually be sharp?
questions.memo: G major sharpens F to F# throughout.

questions.question: If a piece is in F major, which note will usually be flat?
questions.memo: F major flattens B to B flat.

questions.question: A piece in C major contains…
questions.memo: C major has no sharps or flats.

questions.question: Knowing the key helps a player know which sharps or flats to use.
questions.memo: The key tells the player the sharps/flats to apply throughout.

questions.question: You can read music in a key by…
options: singing it in tonic sol-fa or humming the notes
questions.expected: singing it in tonic sol-fa or humming the notes
questions.memo: You can read a melody by singing it in sol-fa or humming the pitches.

questions.question: In G major, every F is played as F-____.
questions.memo: G major raises F to F#.

questions.question: D major uses which two sharps?
questions.memo: D major has two sharps: F# and C#.

questions.question: The same melody can be written in different keys.
questions.memo: A tune can be transposed into different keys, sounding higher or lower.

questions.question: Reading music in a key means the sharps/flats apply…
options: throughout the piece, not just once
questions.expected: throughout the piece, not just once
questions.memo: A key's sharps/flats apply across the whole piece.

questions.question: Which key would have the FEWEST sharps or flats to remember?
questions.memo: C major has none, the simplest to read.

questions.question: In F major, every B is played as B-____.
questions.memo: F major lowers B to B flat.

questions.question: Humming a melody slowly can help you read it correctly in its key.
questions.memo: Humming through helps you hear and check the pitches in the key.

questions.question: If you see one sharp (F#) at the start, the key is likely…
questions.memo: One sharp, F#, points to G major.

questions.question: If you see one flat (B flat) at the start, the key is likely…
questions.memo: One flat, B flat, points to F major.

questions.question: Playing in the wrong key (ignoring the sharps/flats) makes a melody sound wrong.
questions.memo: Leaving out the key's sharps/flats changes the notes and the melody sounds incorrect.

questions.question: Which keys do you read in for Grade 8 Music?
options: C, G, D and F major
questions.expected: C, G, D and F major
questions.memo: Grade 8 focuses on reading in C, G, D and F major.

questions.question: Match each key to its sharps or flats.
questions.expected: C major = none (white keys); G major = F#; F major = B flat.
questions.memo: C none, G has F#, F has B flat.

questions.question: Why is recognising the key useful when learning a new piece?
options: It tells you which notes are sharp or flat before you start
questions.expected: It tells you which notes are sharp or flat before you start
questions.memo: Knowing the key prepares you for the sharps/flats you'll need.

questions.question: If a piece is in F major, the note B is played as…
questions.memo: F major flattens every B to B flat.

CA.G8.MUE.A1.title: Music terminology
CA.G8.MUE.A1.description: Music (CAPS G8) — Listening & elements: Music terminology.
CA.G8.MUE.A1.recovery_strategy: Tempo terms tell you the speed (presto = fast); articulation tells you how to play notes (staccato = short, detached).

questions.question: 'Moderato' is a tempo word meaning…
questions.memo: Moderato means a moderate, medium speed.

questions.question: 'Presto' means…
questions.memo: Presto is a very fast tempo.

questions.question: 'Ritardando' (rit.) means…
questions.memo: Ritardando means gradually slowing down.

questions.question: 'A tempo' means…
questions.memo: A tempo tells you to go back to the original speed (often after a rit.).

questions.question: 'Articulation' in music is about…
options: HOW notes are played — smoothly or detached
questions.expected: HOW notes are played — smoothly or detached
questions.memo: Articulation describes how notes are attacked and joined — smooth or short.

questions.question: 'Legato' means…
questions.memo: Legato means playing notes smoothly, joined together.

questions.question: 'Staccato' means…
questions.memo: Staccato means crisp, short, detached notes.

questions.question: Playing notes smoothly and connected is called ____.
questions.memo: Legato = smooth and connected.

questions.question: Playing notes short and detached is called ____.
questions.memo: Staccato = short and detached.

questions.question: Ritardando and a tempo are both about TEMPO (speed).
questions.memo: Both are tempo terms — slowing down, then returning to speed.

questions.question: Legato and staccato are both about ARTICULATION (how notes are played).
questions.memo: Both describe articulation — smooth versus detached.

questions.question: If a piece marked presto suddenly shows 'ritardando', the music will…
questions.memo: Ritardando slows the music gradually, even after a fast presto.

questions.question: Which term would a composer use to make a section sound bouncy and crisp?
questions.memo: Staccato (short, detached) gives a bouncy, crisp feel.

questions.question: Which term makes a melody sound smooth and flowing?
questions.memo: Legato joins the notes for a smooth, flowing line.

questions.question: 'Presto' means very ____.
questions.memo: Presto = very fast.

questions.question: Musical terms like these are often written in Italian.
questions.memo: Many traditional musical terms come from Italian.

questions.question: After a ritardando, 'a tempo' tells the player to…
questions.memo: A tempo restores the original speed after a change like a rit.

questions.question: Sort each term into TEMPO (speed) or ARTICULATION (how notes are played).
questions.expected: Presto and ritardando are tempo; legato and staccato are articulation.
questions.memo: Tempo = speed words; articulation = how notes are joined or detached.

questions.question: Why do composers write terms like legato and staccato?
options: To tell performers exactly how to shape the notes
questions.expected: To tell performers exactly how to shape the notes
questions.memo: These terms instruct performers on how to play, shaping the music's character.

questions.question: Which term tells a player to gradually slow down?
questions.memo: Ritardando means gradually getting slower.

CA.G8.MUE.A2.title: Elements across styles
CA.G8.MUE.A2.description: Music (CAPS G8) — Listening & elements: Elements across styles.
CA.G8.MUE.A2.recovery_strategy: Every style uses the same elements — metre, dynamics, repetition, contrast — but in its own way.

questions.question: Which of these is a STYLE of music?
questions.memo: Western classical is a musical style; the others are notation or terms.

questions.question: The 'elements of music' you listen for across styles include…
questions.memo: Across any style you can listen for metre, dynamics, repetition and contrast.

questions.question: 'Repetition' in music means…
options: a rhythm or melody that comes back again
questions.expected: a rhythm or melody that comes back again
questions.memo: Repetition is a returning pattern — rhythmic or melodic.

questions.question: 'Contrast' in music means…
options: a clear change, e.g. from soft to loud or slow to fast
questions.expected: a clear change, e.g. from soft to loud or slow to fast
questions.memo: Contrast is a noticeable change in an element — tempo, dynamics, texture.

questions.question: African, Indian, Western classical and popular music can all be described using the same musical elements.
questions.memo: Every style uses metre, dynamics, repetition and contrast — in its own way.

questions.question: Indian classical music often features…
questions.memo: Indian classical music often has a sustained drone and complex rhythmic cycles.

questions.question: African music often features strong use of…
questions.memo: Much African music emphasises rhythm, drumming and call-and-response.

questions.question: A rhythm or tune that returns again is an example of ____.
questions.memo: A returning pattern is repetition.

questions.question: A sudden change from quiet to loud is an example of ____.
questions.memo: A clear change is contrast.

questions.question: The 'meaning of the lyrics' helps you understand…
options: the message or story of the song
questions.expected: the message or story of the song
questions.memo: Lyrics carry the song's message or story.

questions.question: Popular music often uses a repeated chorus, which is an example of repetition.
questions.memo: A repeated chorus is a clear use of repetition in popular music.

questions.question: 'Texture' contrast might be heard when music changes from…
options: one voice to a full choir
questions.expected: one voice to a full choir
questions.memo: Moving from a solo to a full choir is a contrast in texture.

questions.question: Listening across styles helps you appreciate that…
options: different cultures make rich, varied music
questions.expected: different cultures make rich, varied music
questions.memo: Comparing styles shows the rich variety of music across cultures.

questions.question: Metre (the grouping of beats) can be heard in music of any style.
questions.memo: All styles have a metre, even if it differs from Western 4/4.

questions.question: Which pair are BOTH musical styles?
questions.memo: African and popular are styles; the others are note values, dynamics or clefs.

questions.question: When the dynamics change from forte to piano, you are hearing…
questions.memo: A change loud-to-soft is a dynamic contrast.

questions.question: You can compare two songs by listening for their metre, dynamics, repetition and contrast.
questions.memo: These shared elements let you compare any two pieces.

questions.question: Sort each example into REPETITION or CONTRAST.

items.text: The music jumps from soft to loud
A slow section followed by a fast one

questions.expected: Returning choruses and looping patterns are repetition; soft-to-loud and slow-to-fast are contrast.
questions.memo: Repetition = something comes back; contrast = a clear change.

questions.question: Why listen to music from many cultures?
options: It broadens your understanding and appreciation of music
questions.expected: It broadens your understanding and appreciation of music
questions.memo: Listening widely builds appreciation of the world's varied music.

questions.question: A repeated chorus in a pop song is an example of repetition.
questions.memo: A returning chorus is a clear use of repetition.

CA.G8.MUE.A3.title: Instrument families
CA.G8.MUE.A3.description: Music (CAPS G8) — Listening & elements: Instrument families.
CA.G8.MUE.A3.recovery_strategy: Instruments group by how sound is made: chordophones (strings), membranophones (skins), idiophones (the body itself), aerophones (air).

questions.question: Instruments can be grouped by HOW they make their sound. A 'chordophone' makes sound from…
questions.memo: Chordophones (like guitar and violin) sound from vibrating strings.

questions.question: A 'membranophone' makes sound from…
options: a vibrating skin or membrane (like a drum)
questions.expected: a vibrating skin or membrane (like a drum)
questions.memo: Membranophones — drums — sound from a stretched vibrating skin.

questions.question: An 'aerophone' makes sound from…
questions.memo: Aerophones — flutes, trumpets — sound from vibrating air.

questions.question: An 'idiophone' makes sound from…
options: the vibration of its own solid body
questions.expected: the vibration of its own solid body
questions.memo: Idiophones — shakers, xylophone, bells — sound from the whole body vibrating.

questions.question: A guitar is a…
questions.memo: A guitar's sound comes from strings — a chordophone.

questions.question: A djembe drum is a…
questions.memo: A djembe sounds from its skin — a membranophone.

questions.question: A flute is an…
questions.memo: A flute sounds from blown air — an aerophone.

questions.question: A shaker or a xylophone is an…
questions.memo: Shakers and xylophones vibrate as a whole body — idiophones.

questions.question: An instrument that makes sound from vibrating strings is a ____.
questions.memo: Chord = string; chordophone.

questions.question: An instrument you blow into is an ____.
questions.memo: Aero = air; aerophone.

questions.question: A drum and a shaker make sound in the same way.
questions.memo: A drum (skin = membranophone) and a shaker (whole body = idiophone) make sound differently.

questions.question: The word ending '-phone' in these names means…
questions.memo: '-phone' means sound; the first part says HOW the sound is made.

questions.question: A violin and a guitar are both chordophones.
questions.memo: Both make sound from vibrating strings — chordophones.

questions.question: Which family does a trumpet belong to?
questions.memo: A trumpet sounds from blown (buzzed) air — an aerophone.

questions.question: Bells and cymbals belong to which family?
questions.memo: Bells and cymbals vibrate as solid bodies — idiophones.

questions.question: A drum, whose skin vibrates, is a ____.
questions.memo: Membrane = skin; membranophone.

questions.question: Grouping instruments by how they make sound helps us understand them across cultures.
questions.memo: This system (chord/membrano/aero/idiophone) works for instruments worldwide.

questions.question: Sort each instrument into its sound family.
questions.expected: Guitar and violin are chordophones; the djembe is a membranophone; the flute is an aerophone.
questions.memo: Chordophone = strings, membranophone = skins, aerophone = air, idiophone = whole body.

questions.question: Why classify instruments by how they make sound?
options: It works for instruments from every culture, not just the orchestra
questions.expected: It works for instruments from every culture, not just the orchestra
questions.memo: The chord/membrano/aero/idiophone system describes instruments worldwide.

questions.question: A flute, which is blown, belongs to which sound family?
questions.memo: Blown instruments that vibrate air are aerophones.

CA.G8.MUP.A1.title: Creating and composing
CA.G8.MUP.A1.description: Music (CAPS G8) — Performing & creating: Creating and composing.
CA.G8.MUP.A1.recovery_strategy: Composing means making your own music with a clear structure; it can be combined with dance, drama or art.

questions.question: 'Composing' means…
options: creating your own piece of music
questions.expected: creating your own piece of music
questions.memo: Composing is making original music of your own.

questions.question: A composition usually needs a clear…
questions.memo: Good compositions have a clear structure that shapes the music over time.

questions.question: 'Adding another art form' to music could mean…
options: combining it with dance, drama or visual art
questions.expected: combining it with dance, drama or visual art
questions.memo: Music can be combined with dance, drama or art to make a richer work.

questions.question: A composition can be performed by a group or by a soloist.
questions.memo: Compositions can be for solo or group performance.

questions.question: Repetition and contrast help a composition by…
options: giving it shape and keeping it interesting
questions.expected: giving it shape and keeping it interesting
questions.memo: Repetition gives unity and contrast gives interest — both shape a piece.

questions.question: Creating your own original music is called ____.
questions.memo: Composing = creating original music.

questions.question: Which is a good way to START composing a short piece?
options: Choose a steady beat or a short pattern to build on
questions.expected: Choose a steady beat or a short pattern to build on
questions.memo: Starting from a beat or a short motif gives you something to develop.

questions.question: An ostinato can be the foundation that a composition is built over.
questions.memo: A repeated ostinato gives a steady base for other parts to build on.

questions.question: Combining music with dance to tell a story is an example of…
questions.memo: Bringing art forms together (music + dance) integrates them into one work.

questions.question: A 'motif' is…
options: a short musical idea that can be developed
questions.expected: a short musical idea that can be developed
questions.memo: A motif is a short idea (a few notes) that a composer develops through a piece.

questions.question: Performing your own composition lets you share your musical ideas with others.
questions.memo: Performing shares the music you created with an audience.

questions.question: A simple composition structure could be…
questions.memo: A clear structure — intro, main idea, repeat, ending — shapes the piece.

questions.question: Why give a composition a clear beginning and ending?
options: So it feels complete and shaped
questions.expected: So it feels complete and shaped
questions.memo: A clear start and finish make a piece feel whole and intentional.

questions.question: You can develop a motif by repeating it higher, lower, or with a small change.
questions.memo: Developing a motif means varying it — higher, lower, longer, decorated.

questions.question: A short musical idea a composer develops is a ____.
questions.memo: A motif is a short, developable idea.

questions.question: Working in a GROUP to compose, learners should…
options: share ideas and listen to each other
all play different songs at once
questions.expected: share ideas and listen to each other
questions.memo: Group composing needs cooperation, sharing ideas and listening.

questions.question: Composing can use conventional notes OR non-conventional notation like a graphic score.
questions.memo: Compositions can be written in standard notation or with graphic/non-conventional symbols.

questions.question: Put the steps of composing a short group piece in a sensible order.

items.text: Agree on a beat or ostinato
Develop it with repetition and contrast
Shape a clear ending and perform

questions.expected: Agree a beat, make a motif, develop it, then shape an ending and perform.
questions.memo: Build from a foundation up to a finished, performable piece.

questions.question: Sort each into part of COMPOSING or NOT.
questions.expected: Making a motif and adding contrast are composing; buying posters and frames are not.
questions.memo: Composing creates and develops musical ideas.

questions.question: A short musical idea that a composer develops is called a…
questions.memo: A motif is a short, developable musical idea.

CA.G8.VAE.A1.title: Art elements and analogous colour
CA.G8.VAE.A1.description: Visual Arts (CAPS G8) — Art elements & design: Art elements and analogous colour.
CA.G8.VAE.A1.recovery_strategy: Analogous colours sit next to each other on the colour wheel, like blue, blue-green and green.

questions.question: 'Analogous' (related) colours are colours that…
options: sit next to each other on the colour wheel
questions.expected: sit next to each other on the colour wheel
questions.memo: Analogous colours are neighbours on the wheel, like blue, blue-green and green.

questions.question: Which is a set of ANALOGOUS colours?
questions.memo: Yellow, yellow-green and green are neighbours — analogous.

questions.question: Analogous colour schemes usually look…
questions.memo: Because they are related, analogous colours blend harmoniously.

questions.question: Analogous colours are next to each other; complementary colours are opposite each other.
questions.memo: Analogous = neighbours; complementary = opposites on the wheel.

questions.question: The art elements are still…
options: line, shape, tone, texture and colour
questions.expected: line, shape, tone, texture and colour
questions.memo: The elements remain line, shape, tone, texture and colour, now used with more skill.

questions.question: Colours that are neighbours on the colour wheel are ____ colours.
questions.memo: Neighbouring colours are analogous.

questions.question: Blue, blue-green and green together form…
questions.memo: Three neighbouring colours make an analogous scheme.

questions.question: Using related (analogous) colours can give an artwork a unified feeling.
questions.memo: Related colours unify a work and create a calm, harmonious mood.

questions.question: Which element describes how light or dark a colour is?

questions.question: A 'colour wheel' is useful because it…
options: shows how colours relate to each other
questions.expected: shows how colours relate to each other
questions.memo: The colour wheel arranges colours so you can see analogous and complementary relationships.

questions.question: Yellow and purple are analogous colours.
questions.memo: Yellow and purple are OPPOSITE (complementary), not neighbours (analogous).

questions.question: An artist wanting a peaceful, unified sky might choose…
questions.memo: Analogous blues create a calm, unified sky.

questions.question: Mixing a colour with its NEIGHBOUR on the wheel keeps the scheme…
questions.memo: Staying with neighbours keeps colours related and harmonious.

questions.question: Tone and colour can be used together to create depth in a painting.
questions.memo: Lighter/darker tones of colour suggest light, shadow and depth.

questions.question: Which element would you change to make part of a picture look ROUGH?
questions.memo: Texture conveys rough or smooth surfaces.

questions.question: Three colours next to each other, like red, red-orange and orange, form an ____ scheme.
questions.memo: Neighbouring colours make an analogous scheme.

questions.question: By Grade 8 you use the same art elements as Grade 7 but with more control and complexity.
questions.memo: The elements stay the same; your skill and complexity grow.

questions.question: Sort each colour pairing into ANALOGOUS or COMPLEMENTARY.
questions.expected: Neighbouring colours are analogous; opposite colours are complementary.
questions.memo: Analogous = next to each other; complementary = opposite on the wheel.

questions.question: Why might an artist choose an analogous colour scheme?
options: To create a calm, harmonious and unified feeling
To make the strongest possible contrast
